trial_name: BLING III — Continuous vs Intermittent β-Lactam Antibiotic Infusions in Critically Ill Patients With Sepsis (2024)
citation: Dulhunty JM, Brett SJ, De Waele JJ, et al; BLING III Study Investigators and the ANZICS Clinical Trials Group. Continuous vs intermittent β-lactam antibiotic infusions in critically ill patients with sepsis: the BLING III randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2024;332(8):629-637.
trial_type: RCT — international, multicentre, pragmatic, phase 3, open-label, parallel-group randomised clinical trial (1:1)
one_liner: Continuous infusion of piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem did not significantly reduce 90-day mortality in the primary unadjusted analysis (24.9% vs 26.8%, p=0.08) but significantly improved 14-day clinical cure.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients with sepsis prescribed piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem with at least 1 organ dysfunction criterion.
pico.intervention: Continuous infusion of clinician-determined total 24-hour dose of piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem for duration of treatment or until ICU discharge.
pico.comparison: Intermittent infusion (nominally over 30 minutes) of clinician-determined dose of piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem.

background.existing_knowledge: Beta-lactam antibiotics exhibit time-dependent bacterial killing, requiring free-drug concentrations to remain above the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Critical illness induces altered volume of distribution, augmented renal clearance, and organ dysfunction, leading to inadequate exposure with intermittent dosing.
background.knowledge_gap: Prior RCTs and meta-analyses suggested potential benefits in clinical cure and mortality with continuous infusions but were limited by small sample sizes and methodological quality, leaving guidelines conditional.
background.hypothesis: Continuous infusion of piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem reduces all-cause 90-day mortality compared with intermittent infusion in critically ill adults with sepsis.

methods.design: International, multicentre, pragmatic, phase 3, open-label, 1:1 parallel-group randomised trial.
methods.setting: 104 adult ICUs in Australia, Belgium, France, Malaysia, New Zealand, Sweden, and the UK from 2018 to 2023.

inclusion: Adult ICU patients (age >=18 years) with suspected or documented infection
Commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem for current episode
At least 1 organ dysfunction criterion within preceding 24 hours (MAP <60 mmHg >=1h, vasopressors >4h, HFNO/CPAP/BiPAP/IMV >=1h, or serum creatinine >220 umol/L)
exclusion: Receipt of piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem for >24 hours for current episode
Known allergy to study antibiotics or penicillin
Limitations of advanced life support over next 48 hours

methods.intervention: Continuous infusion of clinician-determined total 24-hour dose of piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem. Switching agents permitted with intermittent loading dose.
methods.comparison: Intermittent infusion (nominally over 30 minutes) of clinician-determined dose. Switching agents permitted.
methods.blinding: Open-label for treating clinicians and bedside staff; primary endpoint was objective (mortality).
methods.sample_size_power: 7000 patients required for 90% power to detect 3.5% absolute reduction in 90-day mortality (27.5% to 24.0%) at 2-sided alpha 0.05, allowing 5% withdrawal.
methods.primary_outcome: All-cause mortality at 90 days after randomisation.
secondary_outcomes: New acquisition, colonisation, or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms or Clostridioides difficile at day 14
Kidney replacement therapy-free days to day 90
methods.follow_up: Day 14 for clinical cure and resistant pathogens; Day 90 for primary mortality and organ-free days.

headline_bullets: Unadjusted primary 90-day mortality was lower with continuous infusion (24.9% vs 26.8%) but did not reach statistical significance (OR 0.91, p=0.08).
Prespecified adjusted mortality model reached statistical significance (OR 0.89, p=0.04).
Clinical cure at day 14 was significantly higher with continuous infusion (55.7% vs 50.0%, OR 1.26, p<0.001).
No significant difference was observed in MDRO/C. difficile acquisition or adverse event rates.

outcomes_table.note: Adjusted for sex, APACHE II, admission source, and baseline beta-lactam; ARD −2.2% (95% CI −5.5 to 1.1)
Absolute difference 5.7% (95% CI 2.4 to 9.1); Holm-Bonferroni adjusted

outcomes_table.outcome: New MDRO or C. difficile acquisition/colonisation/infection (day 14)
New MDRO acquisition excluding C. difficile (day 14)
Days alive and free of ICU (to day 90)
Days alive and free of hospital (to day 90)
outcomes_table.note: Tertiary outcome; confidence interval excludes 0 despite adjusted P value

outcomes_table.outcome: Days alive and free of mechanical ventilation (to day 90)
Days alive and free of KRT (to day 90)

subgroup_table.subgroup: Prespecified subgroups (pulmonary/non-pulmonary, drug, age, sex, APACHE II)

safety: Any adverse event occurred in 10/3466 (0.3%) in continuous vs 6/3484 (0.2%) in intermittent group.
One serious adverse event occurred in the continuous infusion group assessed as possibly related.

domains.notes: Centralised encrypted web-based randomisation using minimisation algorithm stratified by study site.
Open-label design. Primary mortality endpoint was objective, but subjective endpoints like clinical cure could be prone to detection or performance bias.
7202 randomised; 171 (2.4%) excluded post-randomisation due to lack of consent; 50 (0.7%) lost to follow-up for 90-day mortality.
Protocol deviations occurred in 31.9% vs 34.1%; incorrect administration method in 8.1% vs 4.8%; dosing/admin delays >1h in 15.3% vs 22.6%.
Well balanced: mean age 59.3 vs 59.6, APACHE II 19.6 vs 19.5, vasopressors 71.0% vs 70.3%, pulmonary source 59.0% vs 60.0%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong with central randomisation and high mortality follow-up, though attenuated by open-label design and non-trivial protocol contamination.

domains.notes: High generalisability to adult ICU sepsis patients with organ dysfunction receiving common broad-spectrum beta-lactams in developed healthcare systems.
104 ICUs across 7 countries; requires appropriate IV access, infusion pumps, pharmacy stability considerations, and nursing workflows.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for general adult ICU sepsis populations, though limited for patients on dialysis at baseline or settings with severe operational constraints.

strengths: Largest randomised trial to date evaluating beta-lactam infusion strategies in ICU sepsis
Pragmatic multi-center international design across 104 ICUs in 7 countries
High complete follow-up for hard, patient-centred primary mortality outcome (99.3%)
Rigorous prespecified statistical plan including Holm-Bonferroni multiplicity adjustments
limitations: Open-label design creates potential bias for secondary clinician-assessed outcomes like clinical cure
Non-trivial protocol contamination and administration errors (8.1% vs 4.8%) biasing towards null
Exclusion of patients receiving baseline KRT or enrolled >24 hours after antibiotic initiation
Comparator was 30-minute intermittent infusion rather than modern extended 3-to-4-hour infusion

critical_appraisal.summary: BLING III provides robust, large-scale evidence that continuous beta-lactam infusion improves clinical cure and trends toward lower 90-day mortality without increasing adverse events or resistance.
strengths: Enormous sample size (>7000 patients) giving high precision
Pragmatic design evaluating common real-world regimens (pip-tazo and meropenem)
weaknesses: High rates of protocol deviations and baseline continuous infusion exposure prior to randomisation

sections.authors_conclusion: Among critically ill adults with sepsis, continuous infusion of beta-lactam antibiotics did not significantly reduce 90-day mortality compared with intermittent infusion, though clinical cure was increased.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Supports adopting continuous beta-lactam infusion as a preferred administration strategy where logistically feasible, given improved clinical cure and a consistent direction of mortality benefit.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with sepsis or septic shock starting piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Intermittent infusion is unsafe or ineffective if continuous pumps/lines are unavailable.
implementation_caveats: Requires dedicated infusion lines or compatible co-administrations
Requires drug stability verification (especially meropenem multi-hour stability)
Must administer intermittent loading dose prior to starting continuous infusion

controversies.notes: The primary unadjusted analysis did not achieve statistical significance (OR 0.91, p=0.08), whereas the prespecified adjusted model crossed threshold (OR 0.89, p=0.04), generating debate over interpretative hierarchy.
The 5.7% gain in clinical cure (OR 1.26) may be influenced by clinician awareness of group assignment when deciding antibiotic cessation or re-initiation.
Control arm used 30-minute intermittent infusions rather than 3-to-4-hour extended infusions now popular in many ICUs.

context_related_trials.relation: MERCY evaluated continuous vs intermittent meropenem in 607 ICU patients with sepsis/septic shock and found no difference in 28-day mortality or PDR/XDR resistance, but showed concordant non-significant trends favoring continuous infusion.

unresolved_questions: Does continuous infusion offer distinct mortality advantages over extended (3-4 hour) intermittent infusion?
What is the impact of routine Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM) combined with continuous infusion on clinical outcomes?
Are specific sub-populations (e.g., augmented renal clearance, high MIC pathogens) driving the clinical cure benefit?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Continuous beta-lactam infusion improves 14-day clinical cure and trends toward reduced 90-day mortality in ICU sepsis without added toxicity.
